summary:
H.R. 7757, the "Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act" or "KIDS Act," establishes a regulatory framework to protect minors (defined as individuals under 17) online, imposing duties on covered platforms, online video game providers, and chatbot providers, and directing federal research and education initiatives. The Act generally takes effect one year after enactment, with specific exceptions.

Title I (the "SCREEN Act") requires providers of covered platforms, defined as those where more than one-third of material is sexual material harmful to minors, to adopt technology verification measures to identify and prevent minors from accessing such material within one year of enactment. It preempts state laws requiring similar verification measures.

Title II, Subtitle A (the "Kids Online Safety Act") mandates that covered platforms implement policies to address specified harms to minors, including physical violence, sexual exploitation, and illegal drug distribution. It requires platforms to provide safeguards and parental tools, defaulting to the most protective settings, and prohibits advertising of illegal products to minors. Platforms must conduct annual independent audits and submit reports to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

Title II, Subtitle B (the "Safe Messaging for Kids Act") prohibits ephemeral messaging features for minors and direct messaging for children under 13. It requires parental controls for direct messaging features for teens, effective 180 days after enactment, except for section 235 (parental controls).

Title II, Subtitle C (the "SPY Kids Act") restricts market or product-focused research on minors, effective 90 days after enactment.

Title III (the "Safer GAMING Act") requires online video game providers to implement communication safeguards and other protective tools for minors, enabled by default.

Title IV (the "SAFE BOTs Act") prohibits chatbot providers from falsely representing chatbots as licensed professionals to minors, requires AI and crisis resource disclosures, and mandates policies to address prolonged use and harmful content.

Title V directs the FTC and the Department of Health and Human Services to conduct studies and issue reports on social media use, fentanyl access, safety tools, and chatbot mental health impacts. It amends the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) to require FTC public awareness campaigns and establishes the Kids Internet Safety Partnership within the Department of Commerce, which sunsets five years after its establishment.

Title VI treats violations as unfair or deceptive acts under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, providing for FTC and state attorney general enforcement. It vests exclusive jurisdiction for constitutional challenges in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, with a 90-day statute of limitations for facial challenges and 60 days for as-applied challenges. It includes rules of construction preserving encryption standards and leaving Section 230 of the Communications Act of 1934 unaltered.
